_note: First-person accounts this site may lawfully reproduce. 'public-domain' entries are quoted at length from the original text. 'excerpt' entries are short quotations from a published source, used with citation. 'summary' entries describe a published account in our own words and link to it, because its text is not ours to reproduce. The two large archives, NDERF and IANDS, are linked and never copied: NDERF's terms forbid redistribution and IANDS states it cannot grant permission to quote its public accounts.

accounts.source: Plato, Republic, Book X, c. 380 BC. Benjamin Jowett translation, Project Gutenberg.
accounts.text: He was slain in battle, and ten days afterwards, when the bodies of the dead were taken up already in a state of corruption, his body was found unaffected by decay, and carried away home to be buried. And on the twelfth day, as he was lying on the funeral pile, he returned to life and told them what he had seen in the other world. He said that when his soul left the body he went on a journey with a great company, and that they came to a mysterious place at which there were two openings in the earth; they were near together, and over against them were two other openings in the heaven above. In the intermediate space there were judges seated… He drew near, and they told him that he was to be the messenger who would carry the report of the other world to men, and they bade him hear and see all that was to be heard and seen in that place.
accounts.note: The oldest surviving Western narrative of this shape: leaving the body, a journey with others, a place of judgment, a pillar of light, and being appointed to go back and tell what he saw. Plato frames it as a tale rather than a report, and Er is a Pamphylian, not an Athenian.

accounts.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book V, Chapter XII; event c. 696, written c. 731. Revised A. M. Sellar translation (1907), after Giles and Stevens. Project Gutenberg.
accounts.text:
This man fell sick, and his sickness daily increasing, he was brought to extremity, and died in the beginning of the night; but at dawn he came to life again, and suddenly sat up, whereat all those that sat about the body weeping fled away in great terror, only his wife, who loved him better, though trembling and greatly afraid, remained with him. And he comforting her, said, “Fear not, for I am now in very deed risen from death whereof I was holden, and permitted again to live among men; nevertheless, hereafter I must not live as I was wont, but after a very different manner.”

[He divided his property, moved to Melrose and took the tonsure. Then:]

“He that led me had a countenance full of light, and shining raiment, and we went in silence, as it seemed to me, towards the rising of the summer sun. And as we walked we came to a broad and deep valley of infinite length; it lay on our left, and one side of it was exceeding terrible with raging flames, the other no less intolerable for violent hail and cold snows… I began to think that peradventure this might be Hell, of whose intolerable torments I had often heard men talk. My guide, who went before me, answered to my thought, saying, ‘Think not so, for this is not the Hell you believe it to be.’”
accounts.note: A guide of light, a journey, a boundary, and a life changed completely on return: he gave away everything he owned and became a monk. The guide answering his unspoken thought is a detail modern accounts still report. Bede also has darkness thickening and then 'the brightness of a star shining amidst the darkness' coming rapidly towards him, which is as close as the account comes to a tunnel.

accounts.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book IV, c. 593. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
accounts.text: Stephen dies in Constantinople and is brought before a judge, who refuses him: the wrong man has been summoned, another Stephen of the same name. He is sent back and revives, and the other Stephen is found to have died at that moment. A soldier in the same book sees Stephen again, on a bridge over a dark and smoky river, 'drawn by the legs downward' by terrible men rising out of the water and 'by the arms pulled upward' by white and beautiful persons, the two pulling against each other. Gregory reads the legs and the arms as the man's almsgiving and his unresisted sins of the flesh.
accounts.note: The clerical error, the wrong person summoned by name, turns up again fourteen centuries later in Indian accounts collected by Pasricha and Stevenson. Nobody has explained why. Gregory himself draws no happy ending from it: Stephen never amended his life, and died in the plague a few years later, 'leaving us in doubt whether he were saved or damned'.

accounts.source: du Monchaux PJ, Anecdotes de Médecine, 1740. Rediscovered and reported by Charlier P, Resuscitation 2014;85:e155.
accounts.text: After losing all external sensations, he saw a light so pure and strong that he thought he was in paradise. He perfectly remembered this sensation, and said it was the most pleasant and beautiful he had ever felt in his life.
accounts.note: The oldest known description by a doctor. Bled repeatedly for a fever, the patient lay unconscious long enough to alarm his physicians. Du Monchaux guessed the cause was blood leaving the skin and flooding the brain; today the suspicion runs the other way, towards too little blood and oxygen.

accounts.source: Beaufort F, letter to Dr W. H. Wollaston, written 1825, published 1847.
accounts.text: Beaufort fell into Portsmouth harbour and could not swim. He described the struggle ending in a strange calm, without pain or fear, and then his whole past life appearing to him, not in outline but in detail, every incident in its right place, running backwards and taking, he thought, no time at all. He was pulled out and revived.
accounts.note: The first detailed first-person life review in English, by the man the Beaufort wind scale is named after. He wrote it down 34 years later and it was not published until after his colleague's death.

accounts.who: Albert Heim and more than 20 climbers
accounts.source: Heim A, Notizen über den Tod durch Absturz. Jahrbuch des Schweizer Alpenclub 1892;27:327-37. Translated by Noyes R and Kletti R, Omega 1972;3:45-52.
accounts.text: Heim fell while climbing and survived. He spent 25 years collecting accounts from others who had fallen: climbers, soldiers, workers, a fisherman swept off rocks. He found that about 95% felt no pain and no terror. Instead, thought raced, time stretched, people reviewed their lives, heard music, and felt calm. Several described seeing the whole of their past 'as if on a distant stage'.
accounts.note: The first systematic collection of near-death accounts, made by a geologist, 83 years before Moody's book. It is also the first demonstration that the experience does not depend on the heart stopping.

accounts.source: Pasricha S, Stevenson I. Near-death experiences in India: a preliminary report. Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 1986;174:165-70.
accounts.text: Messengers, called yamdoots, come and take the person away, sometimes roughly. They are brought before a man with a book of records. The book is checked and a mistake is found: the wrong person has been brought, usually someone of the same name from another village. The person is sent back, often against their wish, and a quarter of them wake with residual marks on the body where they were branded in the other realm.
accounts.note: No tunnel appears in any of these cases, and no life review. What the West calls a life review appears here as a record read by someone else.

accounts.source: Feng Z, Liu J. Near-death experiences among survivors of the 1976 Tangshan earthquake. Journal of Near-Death Studies 1992;11:39-48.
accounts.text: Survivors of the earthquake that killed about 240,000 people were traced and interviewed eleven years later. Forty per cent met the criteria for an NDE. They described time slowing, thought speeding up, a sense of leaving the body and of unusual clarity, and meeting people. A life review was reported by half of them, and a tunnel-like dark region by one in six.
accounts.note: Feng and Liu read their results as culturally distinct from American and Indian accounts. Kellehear, reviewing the same table, read it the other way: out-of-body sensations, tunnel sensations, peace, life reviews, deceased beings and another realm were all reported, so 'the Chinese NDE may be very similar to the Anglo-European NDE'. Both readings are of the same 81 interviews.

accounts.source: Green JT. Near-death experiences in a Chammorro culture. Vital Signs 1984;4(1-2):6-7, as summarised in Kellehear A, Census of non-Western near-death experiences to 2005. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2008;26:249-65.
accounts.text: People report leaving the body and flying through the clouds, or finding themselves walking on a road. Some make invisible visits to living relatives in America. They arrive at a gardenlike, paradisiacal place and are met by the dead, some of them relatives. There is no tunnel and no review of the life.
accounts.note: One of the small set of non-Western accounts in which an out-of-body sensation is clearly reported. Green's original article in the IANDS newsletter has never been digitised, so every detail here comes through Kellehear.

accounts.source: King M, Being Pakeha: An Encounter with New Zealand and the Maori Renaissance, 1985, pp. 92-94. Quoted in Kellehear A, An Hawaiian near-death experience. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:31-35.
accounts.text: She hovers over her own head, leaves the room and flies north, over the Waikato River and the Manukau and across Ngati Whatua, Ngapuhi, Te Rarawa and Te Aupouri, until she reaches Te Rerenga Wairua, the leaping off place of spirits at Cape Reinga. She performs ablutions and dances before the entrance. A voice stops her, saying her time has not come and she must return until called again. She wakes to her anxious living relatives around her.
accounts.note: The journey follows an actual geography the culture already holds, named river by river, rather than a tunnel. What turns her back is a voice, not the dead.

accounts.source: Bailey LW. A 'little death': the near-death experience and Tibetan delogs. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;19:139-59.
accounts.text: A person is taken for dead, sometimes for days. Guides lead them through the Buddhist realms, hot and cold. Their deeds are weighed in public: a demon holds black pebbles for the sinful deeds, a white deity holds white pebbles to weigh against them, and there is a bridge, a scale, and the mirror of existence. They are sent back with a message for the living, usually to practise and to stop causing harm.
accounts.note: A tradition centuries old. Bailey's named cases are Sangs Rgyas Chos 'dzom, a twelve-year-old Bhutanese girl writing shortly after 1650, and Dawa Drolma (c. 1900-1941). No tunnel; the life review is a public reckoning rather than a private film.

accounts.who: 154 people who wrote their accounts down
accounts.source: Martial C et al. Temporality of features in near-death experience narratives. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2017;11:311. Open access (CC BY).
accounts.text: People wrote down what happened in their own words; the researchers coded each account for which features it contained and in what order. Peace was reported by 80%, a bright light by 69%, meeting beings by 64%, leaving the body by 53%. Leaving the body was most often the first thing to happen and returning the last, but the middle varied from person to person. The familiar sequence of out-of-body, tunnel, light, peace appeared in only 6 of the 27 accounts that contained all four.
accounts.note: The study that undid the idea of a fixed script.

accounts.source: Cassol H et al. A systematic analysis of distressing near-death experience accounts. Memory 2019;27:1122-29.
accounts.text: Fourteen per cent of the accounts were distressing, and fell into three kinds: the usual features experienced as threatening rather than welcoming; frankly hellish scenes; and the void, an empty nothingness with no light and no presence at all, which people found the hardest of the three to live with afterwards.
accounts.note: The part of the subject most often left out. It is on this site because leaving it out would be a lie about the evidence.

linked_archives.name: NDERF
linked_archives.what: Over 16,000 first-person accounts across its three sites, each with a long structured questionnaire, in more than 30 languages. The largest public archive there is.
linked_archives.why_not_here: Accounts are under joint copyright with each contributor, and NDERF's terms forbid redistribution. Many contributors gave permission for their account to appear on NDERF and nowhere else.

linked_archives.name: IANDS
linked_archives.what: Hundreds of public accounts, plus a private Experience Registry open to researchers under an access agreement.
linked_archives.why_not_here: IANDS states that it cannot grant permission to publish quotations from the accounts people shared with it.

linked_archives.name: Journal of Near-Death Studies
linked_archives.what: The field's own journal, 1,081 items from 1982 to 2025, free to read. Most of the case material on this page comes from here.
linked_archives.why_not_here: Readable in full at the link; this site quotes short passages with citation rather than reproducing articles.
